guideTitle: Best Electric Trolling Motors for Kayaks (2026)
metaTitle: Best Electric Trolling Motors for Kayaks (2026)
metaDescription: Six electric trolling motors for kayaks compared by thrust, voltage, weight, shaft length, brushless or brushed design and battery needs for small paddle craft.
expertTake: The Newport Kayak Series 36 lb is the pick for most kayaks, with a 24 inch shaft and eight speeds on a single 12 volt battery. The Newport NK180 HD is the pick for anglers who want brushless power on a 24 volt lithium system, and the BKC motor is the light option at 14.3 pounds. A kayak needs far less thrust than any marketing number suggests, so battery weight is the constraint.
introParagraphs: A kayak weighs a fraction of a fishing boat, and that changes every number in a trolling motor spec. The usual rule of 2 pounds of thrust per 100 pounds of loaded boat weight puts a 400 pound kayak and angler at only 8 pounds of thrust, so a 36 or 55 pound motor is an enormous margin that mostly buys speed and wind resistance, not necessity.

What limits a kayak motor is weight and mounting. The battery is often heavier than the motor, the motor must clear the paddle stroke, and the whole setup must keep the kayak stable. This guide ranks the lineup by weight, shaft length, voltage and drive design, and treats raw thrust as a secondary measure.

products.name: Newport Kayak Series 36 lb Thrust Saltwater Trolling Motor, 24 In. Shaft
products.description:
Newport's Kayak Series 36 pound motor is designed for kayaks and canoes, with a transom mount, a short 24 inch shaft, eight speeds, a 6 inch telescoping tiller and an LED battery indicator. The aluminum motor head uses corrosion-resistant magnesium, zinc and other metals, and the unit is saltwater-rated.

The 24 inch shaft is the right length for a kayak, where the mount sits only a few inches above the waterline. A longer shaft drags and risks hitting the bottom in shallow water. The 36 pounds of thrust is far more than a loaded kayak needs by the usual rule, which means the motor runs easily at low speeds and spares the battery. Eight speeds give fine control, and the LED meter shows the battery level at a glance.

A transom-mounted motor needs a mounting plate or a kayak with a motor bracket, and the tiller handle sits near your hip. Use a small 12 volt deep cycle or lithium battery, keep it secured and dry, and fuse the line. Rinse the motor after saltwater use and check the prop for line. Before the first trip, test the setup at the dock: sit in the kayak, lower the motor and check that the prop stays submerged when you shift your weight, that the tiller clears your leg and that the cable run is neat and out of your paddle path. A tidy installation makes the day on the water safer.
products.bestFor: Kayak anglers who want a proven, short-shaft transom motor.
pros: Eight speeds with an LED battery meter
Telescoping tiller adjusts to your position
cons: Needs a motor mount or bracket
Brushed motor is less efficient than brushless
Thrust is far more than a kayak needs

products.name: Newport NK180 HD 24V Electric Kayak Motor, 65 lb Thrust, Brushless
products.description:
The NK180 HD is a 24 volt brushless motor with a listed 600 watts, 1.8 horsepower and 65 pounds of thrust, and it requires a 24 volt LiFePO4 lithium battery sold separately. Brushless direct drive gives smooth, quiet power with variable speed.

Brushless is the technology to look for. A brushless motor has no brushes to wear, runs cooler and wastes less energy as heat, which stretches a small battery's range, and direct drive removes the gearbox noise that angers fish and neighbors. A 24 volt system draws about half the current of a 12 volt one for the same power, which means thinner cable heat and longer runtime.

The trade-off is cost and the battery requirement: you must buy a 24 volt lithium battery, which is lighter than lead-acid but still a significant purchase. Use a battery with a built-in management system, mount it low and secure, and keep the connectors dry. It is the most capable and most efficient motor in this guide, and it suits anglers who cover long distances.
products.bestFor: Anglers who want brushless efficiency and range on a 24 volt lithium system.
pros: Brushless direct drive is quiet and efficient
cons: Requires a 24 volt LiFePO4 battery sold separately
Costs more than brushed 12 volt motors

products.name: PARKHO HASWING W40 12V 40 lb Brushless Kayak Motor, Kill Switch
products.description:
The Haswing W40 is a 12 volt brushless kayak motor with 40 pounds of thrust, five forward and five reverse speeds and an emergency kill switch. Compatibility with the Hobie ProAngler series is stated, along with suitability for diverse waterways.

Brushless efficiency at 12 volts is the combination that stands out. You get the lower heat and longer life of a brushless motor without the 24 volt battery requirement. Five reverse speeds, matching the forward speeds, are unusual and useful when you need to back away from a snag or a dock. The emergency kill switch cuts power instantly if you fall out or the kayak tips, which is a genuine safety benefit.

Compared with the Newport Kayak Series, the Haswing is brushless and has a kill switch, but offers less saltwater detail in the text reviewed. Confirm the mounting method for your kayak, use a secured 12 volt battery and keep the kill lanyard attached to your wrist or life jacket. Rinse after use.
products.bestFor: Kayak anglers who want brushless efficiency and a kill switch on 12 volts.
pros: Five forward and five reverse speeds
Compatible with Hobie ProAngler per the listing

products.name: BKC Kayak Trolling Motor for Sit-On-Top Fishing Kayaks

specList.label: Noise
specList.value: Quiet at full power per the maker

products.description:
BKC's kayak motor weighs just 14.3 pounds, so the overall vessel weight barely rises, and the maker says it runs quiet and smooth even at full power so it will not scare fish. Five forward and three reverse speeds pair with responsive steering, and the motor is designed for sit-on-top fishing kayaks.

Weight is the point. A kayak's performance is sensitive to weight, and every pound of motor, bracket and battery matters for portability, loading onto a roof rack and stability. A motor of 14.3 pounds keeps the whole setup manageable, and a quiet motor matters on a still morning.

The listing gives fewer specifics on thrust and voltage than the others, so check the specification page before buying. Mount it securely, pair it with a small battery and use the lower speeds for range. Because the maker markets it for sit-on-top kayaks, check that it fits your hull or transom before you commit. A light motor also reduces strain on the mounting hardware, which lowers the risk of a bracket cracking in chop. Take care to keep the weight balanced, since a motor hanging off the stern raises the tail and changes how the kayak tracks.
products.bestFor: Anglers who haul the kayak alone and want a light motor.
pros: 14.3 pound weight keeps the kayak light
Quiet at full power per the maker
Five forward and three reverse speeds

products.name: Newport Kayak Series 55 lb Thrust Saltwater Trolling Motor, 24 In. Shaft
products.description:
The 55 pound version of Newport's Kayak Series keeps the 24 inch shaft, the eight speeds, the 6 inch telescoping tiller and the corrosion-resistant aluminum head of the 36 pound motor, and adds more thrust. Kayak and canoe propulsion is its stated purpose, and saltwater use is within its rating.

The extra thrust is mostly headroom. A loaded kayak needs only a few pounds by the usual rule, so 55 pounds helps in strong wind, current or when towing a second kayak, but it draws more current at full speed and rarely runs at full. If you fish open water with wind and tide, the margin has value, and if you paddle ponds, the 36 pound motor is enough.

The heavier motor is a bit harder to mount on a lightweight kayak, so check the transom plate rating. Use a 12 volt battery sized for the draw, keep the motor rinsed and fuse the cable. For larger canoes and tandem kayaks, it is a sensible step up.
products.bestFor: Tandem kayaks and open-water paddlers who want extra headroom.
pros: 55 lb thrust for wind and current
cons: Higher current draw at full power
More thrust than most kayaks need

products.name: 40 lb Thrust Brush Electric Trolling Motor, 12V, Telescopic Handle

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Built-in circuit breaker, LED battery light

products.description:
This motor has a solid copper brush design with 40 pounds of thrust on 12 volts, five forward and three reverse speeds, a telescopic handle and an adjustable depth and angle for small boats. An LED light at the top shows battery power, and a built-in circuit breaker protects the motor.

The built-in circuit breaker is a thoughtful safety touch: it trips if the prop jams or the current spikes, which protects the motor and the battery. The telescopic handle lets you set the length for a seated position, and the adjustable depth and angle make it flexible for different hulls. The listing's shaft range of about 19 to 24.5 inches suits a kayak.

A brushed motor is less efficient than a brushless one and wears over time, so expect to service it, but it is a simple, repairable design and costs less. Mount it securely, use a fused battery and rinse after saltwater use. For a budget kayak setup, it is a reasonable starting point. A brushed motor is also easy for a handy owner to service, with replacement brushes available for many designs, and it makes a sensible first motor while you learn how much power you really use. Keep the brush housing dry and listen for a rough sound, which signals worn brushes.
products.bestFor: Budget-minded kayakers who want a simple brushed motor with a breaker.
pros: Five forward and three reverse speeds
cons: Brand and saltwater rating are unclear

buyingCriteria.explanation: The usual rule of 2 pounds of thrust per 100 pounds of loaded boat means a 400 pound kayak and angler needs only about 8 pounds. The 36, 40, 55 and 65 pound motors here all exceed that, so extra thrust is margin for wind and current, not a requirement. Do not pay for thrust you will not use at full speed.

The BKC weighs 14.3 pounds, and a lead-acid battery can weigh more than the motor. Weight affects stability, portability and loading on a roof rack. Lithium batteries cut weight at a higher cost. As an example, a lead-acid deep cycle battery big enough for a day on the water can add well over thirty pounds, which is nearly twice the BKC motor, while a lithium battery of similar capacity weighs roughly a third as much. Put the battery low and near the center of the kayak so the hull stays balanced.

The Newport Kayak Series and Haswing W40 run on 12 volts, while the NK180 HD needs 24 volts and a LiFePO4 lithium battery. Higher voltage draws fewer amps for the same power. A 12 volt system is simpler and cheaper.

The Haswing W40 and NK180 HD are brushless, while the 40 pound motor is brushed. Brushless motors run cooler, last longer and use energy more efficiently. Brushed motors are simpler and cheaper but wear.

The Newport Kayak Series uses a 24 inch shaft, and the 40 pound motor adjusts from about 19 to 24.5 inches. A kayak mount sits near the waterline, so a short shaft avoids dragging. Confirm that your kayak has a transom, a bracket or a motor mount.

The Haswing W40 has an emergency kill switch and the 40 pound motor a circuit breaker, while the Newport models are saltwater-rated. A kill switch protects you if you fall in. Rinse every motor after use.

faq.q: How much thrust does a kayak need?
faq.a: Only a few pounds by the usual rule of 2 pounds per 100 pounds of loaded weight, so a 400 pound kayak and angler need about 8 pounds. Larger motors give margin for wind, current and towing, and they let you run at a fraction of full power, which saves battery. Treat 36 to 55 pounds as comfortable, and do not pay extra for more than you will use.

faq.q: Do I need a 24 volt system?
faq.a: Not for most kayaks. A 12 volt motor needs one battery, which keeps the setup light and cheap. A 24 volt system draws fewer amps for the same power, which helps range and cable heat, and it suits brushless motors like the NK180 HD, but it needs a matching lithium battery and a bigger investment.

faq.q: Can I mount a trolling motor on any kayak?
faq.a: No. You need a transom, a bracket or a motor mount designed for your hull, and the mount must handle the motor's weight and thrust. Many fishing kayaks offer accessory mounts, but a plain recreational kayak may need a clamp-on or a custom bracket. Check the manufacturer's guidance for your kayak before you drill or clamp anything.

faq.q: How long will the battery last?
faq.a: It depends on speed and capacity, and the range is wide. Current draw climbs quickly with speed, so a kayak cruising at a walking pace can run all day on a modest battery while the same motor at full power drains it in an hour or so. A battery meter helps you plan the trip home with margin.

faq.q: Is a lithium battery worth it?
faq.a: It is often worth it in a kayak, since lithium iron phosphate batteries weigh far less than lead-acid of the same capacity, hold voltage steadier and last for many more cycles. The cost is higher up front, and they need a compatible charger and sometimes a battery management system. If you carry the kayak far, the weight saving alone justifies it.

faq.q: Are motors allowed on every water?
faq.a: No. Rules vary by lake, river and region, and some waters restrict or prohibit motors, require registration or limit horsepower and speed. Check the regulations for your waterway before you buy or launch, and carry any required safety gear such as a life jacket and a signaling device.
